newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia's Lebed backs former Yeltsin aide's Duma bid.
newsitem.headline: Russia's Lebed backs former Yeltsin aide's Duma bid.

text.p: Russian security chief Alexander Lebed on Sunday backed ousted presidential bodyguard Alexander Korzhakov's bid for a seat in parliament, heralding what could be a powerful alliance for the post-Yeltsin era.

Lebed, speaking in the arms manufacturing centre of Tula 160 km (100 miles) south of Moscow, promised to support Korzkakov's bid to stand there for election to the State Duma lower house of parliament next February.

"I very much hope that with your help and participation, there will be a worthy successor...," Lebed told a rally in Tula, celebrating the 850th anniversary of its foundation. The two men stood together on a stage during a religious ceremony.
Asked by reporters whom he would support in the election, Lebed named Korzhakov. Asked why, the gruff reserve paratroop general said on NTV commercial television: "I have simply so decided."

The Tula seat, won by Lebed in a December parliamentary election, fell vacant after President Boris Yeltsin named Lebed his national security adviser in June, between the two rounds of the presidential election.

The president sacked the hawkish Korzhakov two days later, dumping a man who had been his tennis, swimming and -- some say -- drinking partner and then picked Korzhakov's political foe Anatoly Chubais as his chief of staff.
An alliance between Lebed and Korzhakov, who once controlled the vast presidential security service, could create a powerful force on the Russian political scene.
It also adds a new twist to rumours of power struggles in the Russian leadership while Yeltsin prepares for heart surgery.
The stocky ex-bodyguard has made no secret of his dislike for liberal economist Chubais, accusing him of seizing the role of regent and acting in an unconstitutional way.
Korzhakov, who was a Kremlin insider and a close Yeltsin ally for many years, has threatened to spill the beans about what he says is top-level corruption within the Kremlin.
He has denied allegations, made by a former top businessman, that he was involved in a multi-million-dollar extortion demand.

Korzhakov, 46, at his first news conference on Friday, said Yeltsin's current entourage had run the president into the ground during the campaign and was now trying to manipulate events behind his back.
"What we have now is that power, in an apparently legitimate way, has gone into the hands of those never elected in a legitimate way," Korzhakov said, making clear he was referring to Chubais.
Chubais has not yet commented on Korzhakov's allegations.
Korzhakov said on Friday that Lebed had "the best political future in the country" but played down his own importance. A Duma seat would give him immunity from any prosecution.
Lebed, whose main boast in office is a tenuous peace deal in breakaway Chechnya has few allies in the Kremlin.
He took third place in the June 16 first round of Russia's presidential election behind Yeltsin and communist Gennady Zyuganov, winning 15 percent of the vote.
He has made no secret of his presidential ambitions if Yeltsin dies or has to step down early because of ill health.
Yeltsin has spent few of the first 100 days of his second term in office in the Kremlin. He is currently in the Barvikha sanatorium outside Moscow.
